title: False Statement or Omission - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: Learn the severe tax consequences and penalties for a False Statement or Omission on an R&D claim in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: False statements or omissions in Canadian SR&ED claims expose corporations and other taxpayers to serious consequences under the federal Income Tax Act. Misrepresenting routine work as SR&ED can attract gross negligence penalties under section 163, while false or deceptive statements or entries are criminal offences under subsection 239(1.1), carrying fines of 50% to 200% of the excess credit claimed.

body.text: False statements or omissions in Canadian SR&ED claims expose corporations and other taxpayers to serious consequences under the federal Income Tax Act. Misrepresenting routine work as SR&ED can attract gross negligence penalties under section 163, while false or deceptive statements or entries are criminal offences under subsection 239(1.1), carrying fines of 50% to 200% of the excess credit claimed.

Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive and technically rigorous R&D tax incentive architectures, anchored federally by a dual-mechanism system under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations")2. First, Section 37 of the ITA allows taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool eligible current and capital SR&ED expenditures for immediate deduction against business income or indefinite carryforward to future taxation years2. Second, Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA provide an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a 15% basic rate to an enhanced 35% refundable rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures2.

On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, enacting the most significant modernization of the federal SR&ED regime in over a decade3. Applying to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (and to depreciable property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million (generating up to $2.1 million in annual refundable federal credits), broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an alternative three-year average gross revenue phase-out election, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and accompanied the CRA's launch of an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322) on April 1, 20262. Simultaneously, at the provincial level, Québec enacted a major fiscal reform effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing eight legacy R&D tax credits and consolidating them into the fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) at rates of 30% on the first $1 million above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess spending, expanding provincial support to pre-commercialization activities and capital property4.
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2025–2026 Bill C-15 Modernization
1.1 Dual Statutory Foundation Under the Income Tax Act
The federal SR&ED tax incentive program is governed by four interlocking pillars of the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations2:

items: Subsection 248(1) of the ITA (Statutory Gatekeeper Definition): Establishes the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development," enumerating the three core eligible categories—basic research under paragraph (a), applied research under paragraph (b), and experimental development under paragraph (c)—alongside eight permissible categories of commensurate support work under paragraph (d) and seven explicit statutory exclusions under paragraphs (e) through (k)17. Subsection 248(1) also defines critical financial and administrative terms, including "salary or wages," "specified employee," "specified shareholder," and "prescribed" forms7.

Section 37 of the ITA (Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures): Governs the calculation, pooling, deduction, and indefinite carryforward of allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada under subsection 37(1) (as well as permissible salary or wages incurred outside Canada up to a 10% cap under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), and general foreign R&D deductions under subsection 37(2))2. Subsections 37(8) through 37(10) establish the interpretation rules for Canadian SR&ED expenditures, the remuneration caps and bonus exclusions for specified employees, and the annual election to compute overhead via the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)2. Subsections 37(11) and 37(12) enforce the mandatory 18-month reporting deadline for prescribed forms and prescribed information7.

Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA (Investment Tax Credits and Refundability): Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of Investment Tax Credits from Part I tax otherwise payable, while subsection 127(9) defines "investment tax credit," "qualified expenditure," "first term shared-use-equipment," "second term shared-use-equipment," "government assistance," "non-government assistance," and "contract payment"2. Subsection 127(10.1) provides the additional 20% enhanced ITC (yielding the combined 35% rate) for qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), subject to the expenditure limits in subsections 127(10.2) through 127(10.64)2. Subsections 127(18) through 127(20) mandate the reduction of qualified expenditures by assistance and contract payments, subsection 127(26) governs unpaid non-salary amounts under the 180-day rule, and subsections 127(27) through 127(36) enforce the 20-year ITC recapture regime9. Section 127.1 (including subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)) governs the cash refundability (at 100% or 40%) of unused ITCs2.

Sections 2900 to 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations: Regulation 2900(2) delineates directly attributable current expenditures under the Traditional Method; Regulation 2900(4) sets the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate at 55% of the eligible salary base; Regulation 2900(5) establishes the All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more) deeming rule for directly engaged labour; Regulation 2900(6) imposes the Overall Cap on the PPA; Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(10) cap the proxy salary base for specified employees across associated groups (at the lesser of 75% of salary or 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings [YMPE]); Regulation 2900(9) lists mandatory exclusions from the proxy salary base; and Regulation 2903 defines prescribed special-purpose buildings2.

body.text: 1.2 Comprehensive Analysis of the 2025–2026 Bill C-15 Reforms

Following policy consultations initiated in 2024, the Department of Finance Canada announced major structural enhancements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled on December 16, 2024), released technical draft legislative amendments in August 2025, reconfirmed the measures in Budget 2025, and enacted them into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20262.

While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, the August 2025 Department of Finance draft legislative notes, and early tax expenditure summaries initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% rate from $3 million to $4.5 million2, the final enacted provisions of Bill C-15—confirmed by 2026 Department of Finance briefing binders for the Standing Senate Committee on National Finance, Budget 2026 reports, and official CRA SR&ED program updates—doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million3.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and the Two-Step Eligibility Methodology
2.1 Subsection 248(1) Categories, Support Work, and Statutory Exclusions

To qualify for federal tax incentives under Sections 37 and 127, work must satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA6. The opening preamble defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis"19. The definition then divides into three core categories of research and development, an inclusive paragraph for support work, and an exhaustive list of excluded activities20.

Under paragraph (a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, typically carried out in fundamental laboratory settings19. Under paragraph (b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view19. Under paragraph (c), experimental development encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto4. The vast majority of industrial and commercial SR&ED claims in Canada are filed under the experimental development branch of paragraph (c)7.

Once core work under paragraph (a), (b), or (c) is established, paragraph (d) extends SR&ED eligibility to support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight strictly enumerated disciplines: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research, provided that the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer20. Support work never constitutes SR&ED on its own (save for specific non-arm's-length contract exceptions under subsection 37(13)); its eligibility requires satisfying three mandatory conditions: it must fall within one of the eight listed categories, be carried out specifically to perform the related Canadian SR&ED ("directly in support"), and correspond in amount, size, extent, and duration strictly to what is necessary to carry out that SR&ED ("commensurate with the needs")20.
Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude seven categories of commercial and routine activity from the definition of SR&ED20:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion20;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes20;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities20;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas20;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process20;
Paragraph (j): Style changes20; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection20.

body.text: As codified in Section 2.2.2 of the CRA's Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy, the presence of excluded activities within a broader commercial development project does not disqualify the entire project; rather, paragraphs (d) and (e) through (k) define the boundary used in Step 2 of the CRA's review methodology to separate eligible SR&ED work from non-SR&ED work carried out in conjunction with it20. The decisive legal feature distinguishing eligible support work (such as testing or data collection under paragraph (d)) from excluded work (such as routine testing under paragraph (f) or routine data collection under paragraph (k)) is purpose—specifically, why the work was performed and whether it was executed directly to support experimental development or for commercial quality assurance20.
2.2 The "Why" and "How" Requirements and the Five Questions Framework

In August 2021, the CRA updated its administrative guidance to articulate the statutory definition of SR&ED through two foundational requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—while explicitly confirming in its historical guidance notes that both requirements and the five evaluation questions are derived directly from subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the seminal Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC)6.

The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty) governs the purpose of the work6. Work must be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement—that is, generating new knowledge that advances the scientific or technological knowledge base accessible to competent professionals in the field6. Attempting to achieve scientific or technological advancement inherently implies attempting to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty6. In the CRA's analytical framework, advancement is the targeted outcome of SR&ED work, whereas uncertainty is the impetus (motivation) for the work20. A technological uncertainty exists when whether a given technical objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or standard engineering practice ("routine engineering")6. Crucially, the material, device, product, or process being developed is not itself the technological uncertainty, nor does project size or complexity automatically justify an inference that technological uncertainty existed20. Directly adapting a known engineering or technological practice to a new situation where there is reasonable certainty of meeting technological objectives, or performing routine troubleshooting, debugging, and fine-tuning, does not involve technological uncertainty20. However, Question 4 of the CRA's methodology explicitly accommodates advancement not yet achieved: work qualifies as SR&ED even if the targeted advancement is not successfully attained, because experimental failure often reinforces the measure of the underlying technological uncertainty20.

The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search) governs the methodology of the work6. While ordinary commercial R&D follows known design methods, protocols, and standards, the systematic investigation or search required for SR&ED specifically requires a planned, iterative approach comprising four operational stages: (i) observing the subject matter and defining the technical problem along with early-stage indicators and measures to determine whether objectives are met; (ii) formulating one or more hypotheses (defined broadly as an idea, possible solution, proposed method, or approach consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation to prove or disprove that idea); (iii) planning and executing structured experiments or analyses (such as building and testing a prototype in an industrial context) to test the hypotheses and explore relationships between tests; and (iv) developing logical conclusions based on the empirical results, which frequently leads to proposing modified hypotheses in an iterative progression, while keeping organized contemporaneous records generated naturally as the work progresses6.

In both CRA technical reviews conducted by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and Tax Court litigation, Step 1 of the eligibility evaluation applies the Five Questions codified in Section 2.1 of the CRA's Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy6:

items: Question 1 (Section 2.1.1): Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty20?
Question 2 (Section 2.1.2): Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty20?

Question 3 (Section 2.1.3): Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis20?
Question 4 (Section 2.1.4): Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement20?
Question 5 (Section 2.1.5): Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed20?

body.text: 2.3 System Uncertainty, Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP), and Asset Development Rules
Industrial, manufacturing, and software claimants frequently encounter three complex boundary conditions governed by dedicated CRA policies:

System Uncertainty: Recognized in Section 2.1.1 of the CRA's eligibility policy and judicial decisions such as 1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen (2012 TCC 376), 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77), and A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen (2019 TCC 48), system uncertainty is a specific form of technological uncertainty that arises from or during the integration of technologies whose individual components or modules are generally well known7. System uncertainty occurs because unpredictable, adverse interactions between individual components or sub-systems make it impossible to predict how the integrated system will perform20. The locus of the uncertainty is not in the individual modules themselves, but in how they act as an integrated system where the technological specifications of the integrated system cannot be achieved by the underlying sub-system technologies as-is, requiring systematic modification of some or all of the underlying sub-system technologies20.

SR&ED During Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP): Under the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, once SR&ED is established under Step 1, a claimant conducting experimental development on a commercial manufacturing facility must determine the extent of SR&ED under Step 2 by identifying the specific production runs required for SR&ED, the section of the commercial facility involved, the rationale for the production line's involvement, the duration of each run required to evaluate or validate the SR&ED, the personnel performing the SR&ED, and the materials used, isolating SR&ED from excess production or putting a product into a saleable state36. Each necessary production run must be classified based on its facts into one of two contexts to apportion costs36:

items: Experimental Development Resulting in Experimental Production (ED+EP): Applies when there is a genuine technical risk to the process or product attributable to the technological uncertainties, arising mainly from the need to test process parameters (or combinations thereof) outside normal established processes, procedures, ranges, and tolerances36. In an ED+EP context, both directly engaged salaries/wages and the cost of materials consumed in the experimental production are allowable SR&ED expenditures36.

Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP): Applies whenever a production run is part of the experimental development work but does not meet the technical risk threshold required for ED+EP36. In an ED+CP context, all salaries, wages, and material costs usually incurred for normal commercial production must be excluded from the claim; only the excess costs directly associated with the experimental development work are allowable36.

body.text: SR&ED While Developing an Asset (Prototypes, Pilot Plants, Commercial Plants, and Custom Products): Under the CRA's SR&ED While Developing an Asset Policy, when SR&ED involves the design, construction, and testing of a physical asset, the CRA classifies the asset into one of four categories37:

items: Prototypes: Defined as an original model on which something new is patterned—a basic experimental, trial, or preliminary model possessing the essential characteristics of the intended product, built to test the technical feasibility of a concept or hypothesis within a systematic investigation and generally having no lasting commercial value37. Design, construction, and testing expenditures are treated as current SR&ED expenditures, with input materials mostly consumed or transformed37. Constructing duplicate copies of a prototype to build inventory or meet commercial demand is excluded non-SR&ED work; however, duplicate copies constructed strictly for testing prior to commercial production qualify as materials for SR&ED if the testing is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the SR&ED, and their labour, material, and overhead costs are claimed when the copies are consumed or transformed during testing37.

Pilot Plants: Defined as a non-commercial-scale production facility developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED during its useful life, sized specifically for SR&ED, and isolated from normal commercial operations to evaluate hypotheses, establish product specifications, write process formulas, or study raw material behaviour under conditions simulating a full production unit37. If a plant is developed with the intention of temporary or permanent conversion to commercial operations during or after SR&ED, it does not meet the CRA definition of a pilot plant37.

Commercial Plants and Custom Products / Commercial Assets: When SR&ED is performed while developing or modifying a commercial plant or a custom commercial product for a customer, the claimant must use internal accounting controls to isolate the components constructed, segregate SR&ED work from commercial work, and claim only the labour, overhead, contracts, and materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of the SR&ED work37. The CRA explicitly prohibits the practice of claiming 100% of the materials transformed in a custom product or commercial asset and relying on future ITC recapture upon disposition or commercial conversion37. Where it is impossible to isolate the SR&ED work from the construction of a custom product or commercial asset, Section 5.1 of the policy permits an Alternative Approach only if three strict conditions are satisfied: (1) isolating the SR&ED work is impossible, (2) the CRA agrees to the use of the approach, and (3) the claimant signs a formal waiver of the right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the ITA37. Under this Alternative Approach, allowable SR&ED expenditures equal the total actual development costs minus the estimated costs of construction if the technology had already existed, plus the estimated cost of materials transformed in SR&ED37.

body.text: 3. Section 37 Deduction Pool and Section 127 / 127.1 Investment Tax Credit Mechanics
3.1 Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Computing a Canadian SR&ED claim requires executing two sequential but legally distinct calculations on Form T661: first, determining the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under subsection 37(1) (Part 3, Section C of Form T661); and second, determining Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit purposes under subsection 127(9) (Part 4 of Form T661)6. As tax practitioners emphasize, an expenditure can be deductible in the Section 37 pool without producing an ITC in the same amount under Section 127: for example, 100% of an arm's-length SR&ED contract enters Section 37, whereas only 80% enters Section 127; similarly, used ASA capital equipment and non-arm's-length contracts enter Section 37 but do not qualify for an ITC in Section 127; conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is a notional amount used solely to compute the Section 127 ITC and is never added to the Section 37 deduction pool3.

Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, the Section 37 pool operates as a dynamic running balance that gives claimants the optional choice to deduct all or any portion of the available pool in the current taxation year against business income (Line 460), while any remaining positive balance does not expire and carries forward indefinitely to subsequent taxation years (Line 470)10. Furthermore, deducting an accumulated balance from the Section 37 pool in a future taxation year is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, provided the underlying expenditures were properly identified on Form T661 by the reporting deadline for the year in which they were incurred10.

body.text: Two special structural constraints govern the Section 37 pool. First, under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1), when a Loss Restriction Event (LRE) occurs—such as an acquisition of control of a corporation or a new majority-interest beneficiary of a trust—the taxpayer's ability to carry forward unused Section 37 pool balances (including restored capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) acquired on or after December 16, 2024) is restricted, reducing the pool to nil at that time unless reinstated under the continuing business rules in a subsequent taxation year2. Second, under the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, a partnership cannot carry forward any amount in the Section 37 pool to a subsequent fiscal period; any pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal year must be deducted in full when computing the partnership's net business income or loss for that year10.
3.2 Section 127 and Section 127.1 Federal ITC Rates, Expenditure Limits, and Refundability

Under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA, qualified SR&ED expenditures earn an Investment Tax Credit at either the enhanced 35% rate (comprising the 15% basic ITC plus the 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1)) or the basic 15% rate (subsection 127(9))2.
1. Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs)

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, a qualifying CCPC earns the 35% enhanced ITC up to its annual Expenditure Limit2. Under Bill C-15, the maximum annual expenditure limit is $6,000,000 (doubled from the pre-December 16, 2024 limit of $3,000,000)3. Associated corporations (determined by corporate control rules under section 256) must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and allocate it by filing an agreement under subsection 127(10.3)13.

Under subsection 127(10.2), as amended by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit is gradually phased out on a straight-line basis as the corporation's (and its associated corporations') prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada rises from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 (expanded from the historical $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 range), reaching nil when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,0002. Thus, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1 for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,0003. Furthermore, under the Bill C-15 amendments to subsection 127(10.2), a CCPC or associated group whose balance sheet exceeds $15 million in taxable capital (for instance, after raising a large venture capital financing round) may make an annual election for the taxation year so that the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) does not apply, and instead phase out the $6,000,000 expenditure limit using its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding years across the same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 scale2.

Under Section 127.1 (specifically subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)), the cash refundability of a CCPC's unused ITCs depends on whether the expenditures are of a current or capital nature and whether they fall within the expenditure limit2:

items: Current Expenditures Within the Expenditure Limit (100% Refundable): For a qualifying CCPC (as well as a CCPC covered by subsection 127.1(2.01) that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation as defined in 127.1(2)), the 35% enhanced ITC earned on SR&ED expenditures of a current nature up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is 100% refundable, generating up to $2,100,000 in cash refunds per year2.

Capital Expenditures Within the Expenditure Limit (40% Refundable): Under the Bill C-15 amendments to Section 127.1 applying to depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, the rate of refund on the 35% ITC earned on SR&ED expenditures of a capital nature is 40% (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund and 21% non-refundable ITC carryforward)2.

Expenditures Exceeding the Expenditure Limit (15% Basic Rate): Qualifying expenditures in excess of a CCPC's expenditure limit earn the standard 15% basic ITC12. Depending on the CCPC's prior-year taxable income and taxable capital status as a qualifying corporation under 127.1(2), unused 15% ITCs may be eligible for a 40% refund on current expenditures, while non-refundable amounts reduce Part I tax payable and carry back 3 years or forward 20 years2.

body.text: 2. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 amended subsection 127(10.1) and added subsections 127(10.6) through 127(10.64) (while renumbering former subsection 127(10.6) as 127(10.5)) to extend eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to corporations that qualify as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) throughout the taxation year2.

Because public corporations frequently maintain large share-capital balances that would exceed a taxable-capital test, an ECPC's expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.6) is phased out based on gross revenue rather than taxable capital, phasing out for small- and medium-sized Canadian public corporations over the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 range of average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years2. For a standalone (non-consolidated) ECPC, the lookback averages annual revenue reflected in its financial statements over the three fiscal years immediately preceding and ending before the taxation year2. For an ECPC that is a member of a consolidated group, the lookback averages annual revenue over the three fiscal years immediately preceding and ending in the last calendar year that ended before the end of the particular taxation year, using the consolidated financial statements of the "ultimate parent entity" (defined in subsection 127(9) by reference to subsection 233.8(1)) without requiring retroactive adjustments if group membership changed during the 3-year lookback period2. Under subsection 127(10.61), the default expenditure limit for a consolidated group ECPC is nil unless the group files an election under subsection 127(10.62) allocating the group's expenditure limit among member ECPCs (or the Minister allocates the limit under 127(10.63) if the group fails to file within 30 days of a request), with subsection 127(10.64) prorating the limit where an ECPC has two or more taxation years ending in the same calendar year2.
3. Large Corporations, Unincorporated Businesses, and Partnerships

Corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs—such as large public corporations with 3-year average gross revenue of $75 million or more and foreign-controlled subsidiaries operating in Canada—earn the 15% non-refundable basic ITC on all qualified expenditures6. Unused non-refundable ITCs reduce federal Part I tax payable to zero under subsection 127(5) and may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years7. Unincorporated businesses (sole proprietorships and trusts) are not eligible for the 35% enhanced rate, but earn the 15% basic ITC (claimed on Form T2038(IND)) and are generally eligible for a 40% cash refund on unused credits12. Partnerships calculate SR&ED expenditures on Form T661 at the partnership level and allocate the resulting 15% ITC to their partners on Form T5013 slips (accompanied by Form T5013 SUM)24.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Traditional vs. Proxy Overhead Methods
4.1 Annual Election: Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA and Regulation 2900(4), a claimant must select one method—either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method—on Form T661 (Part 3, Section A, Line 160) to compute its SR&ED expenditures for each taxation year9. As set out in the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, this choice is made on a year-by-year basis and is strictly irrevocable for the taxation year once Form T661 is filed40. The Proxy Method must be affirmatively elected on Form T661 when filing the first claim for the year; otherwise, the Traditional Method applies automatically40.

cells: Overhead & Other Expenditures
Not specifically tracked or claimed; replaced for ITC purposes by the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible salary base (Reg. 2900(4))13.
Actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures (Line 360) must be specifically identified, tracked, allocated, and proven to be directly related and incremental to SR&ED (Reg. 2900(2)(c))21.
Impact on Section 37 Deduction Pool
Neither the 55% PPA nor actual overhead is added to the Section 37 SR&ED pool; actual overhead expenses are deducted as regular business expenses under Section 9.
100% of allowable actual SR&ED overhead (Line 360) is included in the Section 37 deduction pool and can be carried forward indefinitely13.
Impact on Section 127 ITC Pool
The 55% PPA (subject to the Overall Cap in Reg. 2900(6)) enters Line 502 as a qualified expenditure, earning federal and harmonized provincial ITCs26.
100% of allowable actual SR&ED overhead enters Section 127 qualified expenditures, earning federal and provincial ITCs13.
Eligible Employee Salaries
Restricted strictly to employees "directly engaged" in SR&ED (hands-on experimentation, analysis, eligible support work, and first-line technical supervision)21.

Includes both "directly engaged" employees (Lines 300/305) AND employees who "directly undertake, supervise, or support" SR&ED (e.g., incremental administrative/clerical support claimed as overhead on Line 360)21.
Cloud Computing, Hosted Services & Lab Utilities
Cannot be claimed separately; deemed to be overhead already represented by the 55% PPA13.

Claimable as overhead on Line 360 to the extent directly related and incremental to SR&ED (e.g., provisioned cloud clusters billed separately for experimental sessions, excluding standing production accounts)13.
Best Suited For
Salary-heavy teams with modest incremental infrastructure where 55% of the salary base exceeds actual incremental overhead13.
Compute-heavy or facility-intensive R&D where actual incremental overhead (such as cloud compute or specialized utilities) exceeds 55% of the salary base13.

body.text: 4.2 Salaries and Wages, "Directly Engaged" Labour, and Specified Employee Caps
1. General Inclusion and Exclusions (248(1) and 37(8))

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA9. It includes regular salaries and wages, fees for services not rendered in the course of business, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honourariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducements, non-competition payments, and—for non-specified employees only—bonuses and remuneration based on profits6. Cash outlays for benefits or non-cash taxable benefits under Section 6 of the ITA can be included in SR&ED salary or wages for Section 37 pool purposes if the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes GST/HST/PST (unless no input tax credit can be claimed), and actual costs are not claimed elsewhere as a business expense21.
Conversely, the following items are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages:

items: Dividends and sole-proprietor/partner drawings, which are returns on shareholdings or equity rather than employment remuneration and can never form part of an SR&ED claim6;
Unpaid founder work where no salary was accrued and paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year9;
Stock option benefits under Section 7 of the ITA, which are considered not to be an expenditure incurred by the employer21;

The employer's share of related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, or group benefit contributions)—under the Proxy Method these are covered by the 55% PPA, whereas under the Traditional Method they may be claimed as overhead on Line 36021;
Expenditures for extended vacation or extended sick leave, during which employees are not considered directly engaged in or directly undertaking, supporting, or supervising SR&ED21; and

Retiring allowances and superannuation or pension benefits (covered by the PPA under the Proxy Method, or claimable as overhead alongside moving/relocation and training costs under the Traditional Method)21.

body.text: Under the Proxy Method, only salaries and wages of employees "directly engaged" in SR&ED qualify21. The CRA defines "directly engaged" based on the hands-on tasks performed rather than job titles: it encompasses employees conducting experimentation or analysis, performing commensurate support work under paragraph 248(1)(d), preparing equipment or materials for experiments (excluding general equipment maintenance), collecting experimental data, and first-line managers or supervisors when directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED work or providing direct technical input21. Time spent by managers on non-technological management activities, supervision beyond the first-line level (unless hands-on SR&ED duties are demonstrated), and clerical or administrative staff (accounting, payroll, finance, legal, purchasing, human resources, reception, and maintenance) is excluded from "directly engaged" labour21. Under Regulation 2900(5), if the portion of an employee's time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more), 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be attributable to SR&ED26.

For permissible SR&ED work performed outside Canada under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), eligible foreign salary or wages claimed on Line 306 of Form T661 are capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salary and wages incurred inside Canada (Lines 300 and 305), allocated between non-specified employees (Line 307) and specified employees (Line 309, which cannot exceed 10% of Line 306 minus Line 307)21.
2. Specified Employees: The 5× YMPE Cap and Bonus Prohibition (248(1) and 37(9) to 37(9.4))

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a "specified shareholder"—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of a related corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the corporation (including indirect ownership via spouses, family trusts, or partnerships, as well as non-arm's-length family members employed in the business)9.
Three mandatory statutory restrictions govern specified employees:

items: Absolute Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): Under subsection 37(9) of the ITA, remuneration based on profits or any bonus paid to a specified employee is strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages9. While a bonus paid to a founder or specified employee may be deductible to the corporation as a general business expense, it earns $0 in SR&ED deductions or tax credits9.

Maximum Allowable SR&ED Salary Cap — 5× YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): Under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed on Line 305 for a single specified employee in a taxation year is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the tax year ends), prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the person was a specified employee9. According to 2026 Canadian payroll and SR&ED guides, the 2026 YMPE is $74,600.00, which establishes a maximum annual specified employee SR&ED salary cap of $373,000.00 ($74,600 × 5) for a full taxation year9.

Associated Corporation Allocation Agreement (Subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4)): If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (for example, an operating company and a founder's holding company), the $373,000 (5× YMPE) salary cap is shared across the group, and none of the specified employee's salary counts in any associated corporation unless all associated corporations file a signed agreement allocating the single cap among them9.

body.text: 4.3 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Calculation and Caps (Regulation 2900)
1. Historical Rate Evolution and Current 55% Rate (Regulation 2900(4))

A frequent compliance error highlighted by Canadian CPA practitioners is applying an outdated 65% overhead proxy rate13. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount rate was 65% in 2012 and earlier, 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% of the eligible salary base since 2014 (including all 2025 and 2026 filings)6.
2. Computing the Proxy Salary Base (Regulation 2900(7), 2900(8), 2900(9), and 2900(10))

The proxy salary base (computed in Part 5, Section A of Form T661, Lines 810 to 820) is narrower than the allowable SR&ED salary claimed in Part 313. First, under Regulation 2900(9) and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, for any employee (whether a non-specified employee on Line 810 or a specified employee on Line 816), the salary base cannot include five mandatory excluded items (entered as a reduction on Line 812 for non-specified employees): (1) taxable benefits under Section 6 of the ITA, (2) unpaid salary or wages from a prior taxation year paid in the current taxation year (Line 310), (3) remuneration based on profits, (4) bonuses, and (5) related employer benefits (along with stock option benefits under Section 7 and deemed-paid vacation pay or salary deferral arrangements)9.
Second, under Regulation 2900(7), the amount a claimant can include in the proxy salary base for each specified employee is restricted to the lesser of9:

items: 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (after excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year); OR

2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, multiplied by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual divided by 365 (note that there is no proration for days in the year when the employee was not a specified employee)9.

body.text: For a full 365-day taxation year ending in 2026 (where the YMPE is $74,600.00), the 2.5 times YMPE proxy salary base ceiling for one specified employee is $186,500.00 ($74,600 × 2.5)9. Under Regulations 2900(8) and 2900(10), if the corporation is associated with another corporation (or a deemed associated individual or partnership) that employed the same specified employee in a taxation year ending in the same calendar year, the total proxy salary base included across all associated entities cannot exceed 2.5 times the YMPE ($186,500.00), and the claimant's cap is reduced by any amount included by the associated corporation9.

To illustrate how the proxy salary base cap operates in practice, consider two startup founders who are specified employees receiving a regular salary of $100,000 each (with no bonus) in 2026, where contemporaneous time records show 70% of each founder's time was spent directly engaged in eligible SR&ED in Canada9:

items: Direct SR&ED Salary per Founder (Line 305): 70% of $100,000 = $70,000 (well below the $373,000 5× YMPE cap)9.

Proxy Salary Base per Founder (Line 816): Capped at the lesser of $70,000 (SR&ED salary), 75% of total salary ($75,000), and 2.5× YMPE ($186,500). Because $70,000 is below $75,000 and $186,500, the full $70,000 enters the proxy salary base9. (Conversely, if a founder had spent 90% of their time on SR&ED on a $100,000 salary, their direct SR&ED salary on Line 305 would be $100,000 under the ASA rule, but their proxy salary base on Line 816 would be capped at 75% of total salary, or $75,000)9.
Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% PPA — Line 502): 55% of $70,000 = $38,500 per founder9.
Qualified Expenditure & 35% Refundable Federal ITC per Founder: $70,000 + $38,500 = $108,500, generating a 35% refundable ITC of $37,975 per founder9.

body.text: 3. Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6))

Under Regulation 2900(6) and Section 4.0 of the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, an Overall Cap ensures that the PPA and other specified deductions do not exceed the total business expenditures deducted in the year26. The Overall Cap is calculated using the statutory formula A minus B minus C, where26:

items: Variable A equals the total of all amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold)26;

Variable B equals the sum of all deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, and bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), Section 26 (for a bank), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (for an insurance agent or broker), Section 37 (SR&ED expenditure pool deduction claimed in the year), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (for a trust)26; and

Variable C equals the total amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as building rent)26. (If a claimant carries on more than one business, the specified deductions from all businesses must be aggregated)26.

body.text: 4.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under paragraphs 37(1)(a) and 127(9) of the ITA and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, materials purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers can be claimed under both the Traditional and Proxy methods when used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada in two specific situations38:

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320): Physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of the tangible "thing" on which the SR&ED is performed, and are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the prosecution of SR&ED38.

Materials Transformed (Line 325): Physical, tangible items that compose the body of the thing on which SR&ED is performed, and are modified or incorporated into an experimental output, prototype, or product that retains value after the SR&ED (rather than being destroyed or rendered virtually valueless)25.

body.text: Three strict audit boundaries govern materials claims under the Materials for SR&ED Policy. First, to qualify as "materials for SR&ED," an item must at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a thing on which the SR&ED is being performed41. Consequently, broken or used laboratory supplies (such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, and pipettes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas, propane), CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants (such as engine oil) do not qualify as materials for SR&ED on Line 320 or Line 325; they are overhead items covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method or claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method41. Second, the cost of materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED (not when purchased into inventory), and materials that would have been consumed in normal commercial production or excess production must be excluded36. Third, Materials Transformed (Line 325) (including recycled SR&ED materials) are subject to the ITC Recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) when the resulting product or fabric is sold or converted to commercial use25.
4.5 Subcontractors (80% Rule, Non-Arm's-Length Rules) and Third-Party Payments
1. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) — Line 340)

When a claimant engages an arm's-length contractor (who must be a "taxable supplier," as amounts paid to a non-taxable supplier are excluded from qualified expenditures on Line 528) to perform SR&ED on behalf of the claimant in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deduction pool (Line 340)22. However, for Section 127 Investment Tax Credit purposes, only 80% of the eligible arm's-length contract expenditure is included in qualified expenditures (enforced by entering a 20% reduction on Line 529 of Form T661)13.

Under Section 6.0 of the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, a claimant may contract out standalone support work (the eight activities in paragraph 248(1)(d)) to an arm's-length performer and claim the contract under either the Traditional or Proxy method if the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed in Canada by or on behalf of the payer22. However, an arm's-length performer contracted to perform only support work cannot claim SR&ED expenditures on its own tax return because support work on its own does not satisfy the definition of SR&ED22. Furthermore, contract costs for non-SR&ED work (such as work by electricians, welders, or mechanics that does not fall under the eight support work categories in 248(1)(d)) do not qualify as SR&ED contract expenditures on Line 340; they are treated as overhead (covered by the PPA under the Proxy Method, or claimable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental to SR&ED)22.
2. Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Section 251, 37(13), 127(9)(f), 127(13) — Line 345)

Where a claimant (payer) enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (Section 251), Section 7.0 of the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy enforces special rules22:

items: Payer Earns No ITC by Default: The payer's expenditure under the NAL contract is an allowable SR&ED expenditure in its Section 37 deduction pool (Line 345), but under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), it is excluded from qualified expenditures (earning $0 ITC for the payer)22. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying allowable and qualified SR&ED expenditures (salaries, materials, etc.), and the amount received from the NAL payer is excluded from the definition of "contract payment" in subsection 127(9) so it does not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures22.

Transferring Qualified Expenditures (Subsection 127(13) — Form T1146): The NAL performer and NAL payer may jointly file Form T1146 under subsection 127(13) to transfer qualified expenditures from the NAL performer (reported as a deduction on Line 540 of the performer's T661) to the NAL payer (reported as an addition on Line 508 of the payer's T661)3. However, the performer cannot transfer more than the amount its qualified SR&ED expenditures would have been at the end of the tax year had it not been for the transfer; if the performer attempts to transfer an excess amount, the Act states that no amount can be transferred39.

NAL Contracts for Support Work Only (Subsection 37(13)): As an exception to the rule that standalone support work is ineligible to a contractor, subsection 37(13) links standalone support work performed by a NAL performer to the related payer's SR&ED so the NAL performer can claim the expenditures22.

Repeal of Subsection 37(14) Look-Through Rule: Consequential on the Bill C-15 restoration of capital expenditures on or after December 16, 2024, subsection 37(14) (which previously restricted expenditures incurred via third-party performers to expenditures of a current nature) was repealed, together with subsection 37(15) (S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5)2.

body.text: 3. Third-Party Payments (Line 370)

Payments made to approved entities, universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada—where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results—are claimed on Line 3706. Exactly like arm's-length contracts, 100% enters the Section 37 deduction pool, while 80% enters Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (with 20% subtracted on Line 529)6.
4.6 Unpaid Amounts — The 180-Day Statutory Rule (78(4) and 127(26))

The ITA enforces a strict 180-day payment window after the end of the taxation year (where payments made on the 180th day are considered timely), operating differently for remuneration versus non-salary expenditures9:

items: Unpaid Salaries and Wages (Subsection 78(4) — Line 315 & Line 310):

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, if accrued salary or wages (for either arm's-length or non-arm's-length employees) remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred, the unpaid remuneration is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year for both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation (removed via Line 315), and is instead deemed to be incurred only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (claimed on Line 310)9.

While a prior-year unpaid salary paid late enters Line 310 for the Section 37 deduction pool and direct salary ITC in the year paid, under Regulation 2900(9) it never enters the proxy salary base and permanently loses the 55% PPA9. (Note: Reasonable vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts under a salary deferral arrangement as defined in 248(1) are deemed paid on the 180th day, though they too are excluded from the proxy salary base)21.
Unpaid Current Expenditures Other Than Salary (Subsection 127(26) — Line 520):

Under subsection 127(26) and Section 4.0 of the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, any current expenditure other than salary or wages (such as an arm's-length subcontractor invoice, materials, or Traditional Method overhead) that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year remains deductible in the Section 37 pool for that taxation year, provided it is identified on Form T661 by the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline9.

However, for Section 127 ITC purposes, 100% of the unpaid expenditure is treated as not having been incurred in that taxation year (subtracted on Line 520) and is added to qualified expenditures only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is paid38.

CRA Policy Example (Section 4.1.1): Suppose B Limited (December 31, 2024 year-end) incurs a $100,000 arm's-length SR&ED contract payable to C Limited that remains unpaid 180 days after year-end and is paid in September 202539. For the 2024 tax year, B Limited reports $100,000 on the arm's-length contract line (Line 340) by the reporting deadline to deduct it in 2024, enters 20% ($20,000) on Line 529 as the statutory 80% contract adjustment, and enters the remaining 80% ($80,000) on Line 520 as an unpaid current expenditure (excluding 100% of the $100,000 contract from 2024 ITC calculations)38. In the 2025 tax year (when paid), B Limited enters 80% of the amount paid ($80,000) on the "payment of prior years' unpaid amounts (other than salary or wages)" line of Form T661 to include it in 2025 qualified expenditures39.

body.text: 4.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were previously removed from SR&ED eligibility after December 31, 20132. Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and lease costs for depreciable property acquired (and becoming available for use) on or after December 16, 2024, and for lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 20242:

items: All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) Capital Property (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390, Part 6B):

Under restored paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, an eligible SR&ED capital expenditure is an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property (available for use after December 15, 2024) for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to the claimant's business, where the claimant intended to either: (i) use All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (ii) consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada2.

Exclusions (Paragraph 37(8)(e)): Non-depreciable assets (such as land), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are explicitly excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures (unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Section 2903 of the Regulations)2.

Interaction with CCA and Used Equipment Rules: Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 are treated as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed under subsection 37(6) and must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (CCA)2. While both new and used ASA depreciable property enter Line 390 and the Section 37 deduction pool, used equipment does not qualify for the Section 127 SR&ED ITC (and is backed out in Part 4, Line 535)3.

Form T661 Part 6B Reporting: Claimants must report their 20 most expensive ASA capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 in Part 6B, entering the name of the property in Box 780, the full capital expenditure acquisition cost (including purchase price, installation, customs, and transportation) in Box 782, and the list of SR&ED project numbers where the property was used in Box 7863.
Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9), Line 504, Part 6C):

Depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if it is used primarily (at least 50% but less than 90% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada3.

The SUE ITC calculation is identical under both the Traditional and Proxy methods: the capital cost of SUE is not part of the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and must instead be depreciated under regular CCA rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH83.

On Line 504 of Form T661, the claimant includes 25% of the capital cost of the equipment in the first period (first-term SUE) and the other 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE) if the equipment meets the primary SR&ED use requirements for each period2. Claimants must report the 20 most expensive SUE expenditures in Part 6C: property name in Box 788, purchase date (YYYY-MM-DD) in Box 790, and 25% of the capital cost in Box 7923.
Equipment Lease Costs (Paragraph 37(8)(a)):

Qualifying lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024 for equipment used ASA (90% or more of operating time after December 15, 2024) in SR&ED in Canada (or used primarily—at least 50% but less than 90%—under the Proxy Method's special equipment rules) once again qualify for SR&ED claims2.

body.text: 4.8 Investment Tax Credit Recapture Rules (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a claimant must report an SR&ED ITC recapture (adding the recaptured credit back to Part I tax payable) when all four statutory conditions are satisfied24:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (subsection 127(36) extends the 10-year period in paragraph 127(27)(a) to a maximum of 20 taxation years to match the 20-year ITC carryforward window)25;
The cost of the particular property was a qualified SR&ED expenditure25;
The cost of the property was included in an amount, a percentage of which can reasonably be considered to have been included in computing the claimant's ITC at the end of the taxation year25; and
In the taxation year, the claimant converts to commercial use or disposes of the particular property or another property that incorporates the particular property25.

body.text: Property subject to the SR&ED ITC recapture rules includes: (i) materials for SR&ED (Materials Transformed) included in a custom product, commercial asset, experimental production, or commercial production with experimental development (including recycled SR&ED materials); (ii) All or Substantially All (ASA) equipment; (iii) Shared-Use Equipment (SUE); (iv) animals and other growing things used in SR&ED projects; and (v) tangible property (other than intellectual property) acquired through an SR&ED contract, including transferred qualified expenditures under subsection 127(13)22.

Crucially, under subsection 127(32) ("Meaning of cost"), the cost of property for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid by the claimant to acquire the property from another person and does not include any amount paid by the claimant to maintain, modify, or transform the property—meaning ITC recapture never applies to in-house labour/salaries or overhead/PPA25. As illustrated in Example 7.1.1 of the CRA's Recapture Policy, if a corporation orders a custom part from an arm's-length supplier for $12,000 ($10,000 manufacturing/development cost plus $2,000 profit), the full $12,000 acquisition cost is subject to recapture upon commercial sale or conversion; whereas if the corporation manufactures the exact same part in-house, there is zero recapture on the in-house salaries or overhead incurred to manufacture it25. Similarly, contracts generating intellectual property do not trigger recapture when the intellectual property (incorporeal property) is sold or commercialized22.

Under Section 5.0 of the CRA's Recapture Policy, a 10% De Minimis Rule prevents recapture in three scenarios: (1) scrap sales where proceeds from selling an experimental product are less than 10% of the total cost of the property; (2) conversions to commercial use (or non-arm's-length dispositions) where the Fair Market Value (FMV) of the SR&ED output is less than 10% of the total cost of the property; and (3) allowed materials consumed costs unless proceeds received (such as insurance payouts) exceed 10% of the cost of the materials25. Any ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added back to the claimant's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the following taxation year under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3) (Line 453 of Form T661)10.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics

In addition to the federal SR&ED incentives, eight Canadian provinces and one territory provide dedicated provincial or territorial R&D tax credits5. All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—except those in Québec (administered by Revenu Québec on Form RD-1029.8.CR with the CO-17 return) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance on the Alberta corporate return)—are administered directly by the CRA through the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return and Schedule 54.
