body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive: Ontario's Three-Tiered R&D Incentive Architecture

Corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario and not exempt from Ontario corporate income tax can stack up to three distinct provincial R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered by the CRA5:

1. Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule 566): The OITC provides an 8% refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% effective June 1, 2016) to qualifying corporations on qualified SR&ED expenditures performed in Ontario up to an annual $3,000,000 expenditure limit (yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000, shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years)11. Following the federal Bill C-15 capital expenditure restoration, the Ontario Ministry of Finance updated the OITC rules (confirmed on October 30, 2026) so that qualified Ontario expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024 remain excluded, and pre-2014 capital expenditures were included at 40%)43. Unlike the federal $6 million CCPC limit, Ontario's $3 million OITC expenditure limit is gradually phased out if either (i) prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, OR (ii) prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,00043.

2. Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 44, Schedule 508): The ORDTC provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% effective June 1, 2016) with no dollar cap, available to all eligible corporations on qualified SR&ED expenditures carried on in Ontario (reduced by government assistance, including any OITC claimed)5. Unused ORDTC credits can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years to reduce Ontario corporate income tax otherwise payable, and converting property to commercial use triggers ORDTC recapture on Schedule 508 (Line 277 of Schedule 5)5. Because the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC constitutes provincial government assistance that reduces federal qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18) of the federal ITA—thereby reducing a CCPC's 35% cash-refundable federal ITC—subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) gives corporations the explicit statutory option to waive the current-year ORDTC, in whole or in part, to preserve immediate federal cash refunds5.

3. Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules 568 & 569): The OBRITC provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an eligible research institute, up to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (shared among associated corporations), yielding a maximum refundable credit of $4,000,000 per year (Line 470 of Schedule 5)5.
5.3 Deep-Dive: Québec's New CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025)

In its 2025–2026 Budget (Québec Finance Bulletin 2025-6), the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive overhaul of its provincial R&D tax incentives, governed by sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act (Québec)4. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished eight legacy R&D tax credits—including the R&D salary and wages tax credit, the university research or public research centre credit, the pre-competitive private partnership research credit, the research consortium membership fees credit, the technological adaptation services credit, and the industrial design credit—consolidating them into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR (or RD-1029.8.CR-T) with the Québec CO-17 corporate income tax return4.
The CRIC introduces four structural transformations for corporations operating an establishment in Québec:

items: Universal Refundability and Two-Tier Rate Structure: The CRIC is 100% refundable for all eligible corporations, regardless of corporate asset size or public/foreign control15. It provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the applicable exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable credit on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 maximum4. (If a corporation claims the CRIC as a member of a partnership, its percentage interest is applied to eligible expenditures, a separate form is required, and the 30% enhanced rate does not apply, restricting the partnership claim to 20%)14.

Harmonized R&D Plus Newly Eligible Pre-Commercialization Activities: While the R&D definitions (basic research, applied research, and experimental development) remain fully harmonized with federal SR&ED legislation and the CRA continues to perform the scientific review of R&D work4, the CRIC newly covers eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with (and as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Québec by the corporation or on its behalf4. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include: (i) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and obtain an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; and (ii) product design, including developing form and aesthetics, improving functionality, selecting materials, competitive market analysis, evaluating operational constraints, prototype development, pilot-user validation, and developing usage scenarios4.

Qualified Expenditures Under the CRIC: Qualified expenditures incurred in Québec encompass: (i) 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees engaged in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities; (ii) 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec; (iii) 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and (iv) 100% of capital property acquisition costs used for eligible work in Québec, excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings (and excluding property used in a Large Investment Project holding a tax holiday qualification certificate)4. Unlike federal SR&ED, the CRIC does not provide a notional proxy overhead allowance47.

Applicable Exclusion Threshold: Before earning the CRIC in a taxation year, a corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an annual Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of: (a) $50,000 (adjusted for the number of days in a short taxation year), OR (b) the sum of the basic personal amount (BPA) of the Québec personal income tax system ($18,751 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026) for each employee, prorated to reflect the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities4.

body.text: 5.4 Government Assistance Stacking and Comprehensive Mathematical Walkthroughs

Under subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) and paragraph 37(1)(d) of the federal ITA, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, provincial super-allowance benefits, and federal/provincial grants or forgivable loans (such as National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program [IRAP] grants) received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date constitute "government assistance" that reduces federal SR&ED pools on a project-by-project basis (with non-arm's-length parties able to allocate assistance via Form T1145 under subsection 127(20))3.
Case Study 1: Ontario CCPC Claiming Proxy Method, OITC (8%), ORDTC (3.5%), and Federal Enhanced ITC (35%)

Consider an Ontario CCPC (with prior-year taxable income under $500,000 and taxable capital under $15 million) that incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged non-specified R&D salaries in Ontario in 2026 and elects the Proxy Method (55% PPA)5:

items: Unadjusted Federal & Ontario Qualified Expenditure Base: Direct SR&ED salaries of $1,000,000 (Line 300) plus the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount of $550,000 (Line 502) equal $1,550,000 in unadjusted qualified expenditures9.

Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC at 8% — Schedule 566): Because $1,550,000 is within Ontario's $3,000,000 OITC limit, the corporation earns a refundable OITC of 8% of $1,550,000 = $124,000 (100% refundable cash)43.
Ontario R&D Tax Credit (ORDTC at 3.5% — Schedule 508):

If Claimed (Option A): Subtracting the $124,000 OITC leaves an eligible ORDTC base of $1,426,000, which multiplied by 3.5% yields $49,910 in non-refundable ORDTC5. Total Ontario government assistance deducted on Line 513 of Form T661 is $124,000 + $49,910 = $173,910, leaving $1,376,090 in net federal qualified expenditures (Line 570)23. At the 35% enhanced rate, the federal refundable ITC is 35% of $1,376,090 = $481,631.502. Total combined federal and Ontario credits equal $655,541.50 (65.55% of the $1,000,000 payroll), consisting of $605,631.50 in immediate cash ($124,000 OITC + $481,631.50 federal ITC) and $49,910 in non-refundable ORDTC carryforwards5.

If Waived Under Subsection 43(1) (Option B): For a pre-revenue startup with no Ontario income tax payable, waiving the non-refundable $49,910 ORDTC under subsection 43(1) means only the $124,000 OITC reduces the federal base, leaving $1,426,000 in net federal qualified expenditures5. At 35%, the federal refundable ITC rises to $499,100, yielding $623,100 in total immediate cash ($124,000 + $499,100)—an immediate cash flow advantage of $17,468.505.

Section 37 Pool Adjustment for Proxy Assistance: Under the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy and Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, while 100% of the Ontario tax credits reduces Section 127 qualified expenditures on Line 513, the portion of the Ontario tax credits attributable to the notional $550,000 PPA does not reduce the Section 37 deduction pool on Line 429; instead, that PPA-related portion is included directly in net income on Schedule T2SCH1 in the taxation year received23.

body.text: Case Study 2: Québec Tech Startup Claiming New CRIC (30%/20%) and Federal Enhanced ITC (35%)

As illustrated in Québec CRIC technical guides, consider a Québec CCPC with $2,000,000 in qualified R&D wages in Québec and one full-time R&D employee (where the $50,000 floor exceeds the single employee's Basic Personal Amount of $18,751 in 2025 or $18,952 in 2026, setting the exclusion threshold at $50,000)15:

items: Québec CRIC Calculation (Form RD-1029.8.CR): Subtracting the $50,000 exclusion threshold from $2,000,000 leaves $1,950,000 in net qualified Québec expenditures4. The first $1,000,000 earns 30% = $300,000, and the remaining $950,000 earns 20% = $190,000, generating a total fully refundable Québec CRIC of $490,0004.

Federal SR&ED Calculation (Form T661 & Schedule 31 under Proxy Method): Direct SR&ED wages of $2,000,000 plus the 55% PPA of $1,100,000 yield $3,100,000 in unadjusted federal qualified expenditures (fully within the modernized $6,000,000 Bill C-15 enhanced expenditure limit)3. Subtracting the $490,000 Québec CRIC as provincial government assistance on Line 513 leaves $2,610,000 in net federal qualified expenditures23. Multiplied by the 35% enhanced refundable CCPC rate, the federal ITC is $913,5002.

Total Combined Refundable Cash: Combining the $490,000 refundable Québec CRIC and the $913,500 refundable federal ITC yields $1,403,500 in total cash refunds—a 70.18% cash recovery on the $2,000,000 R&D salary outlay4.

body.text: 6. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Form T661 Architecture, and Penalties
6.1 Governing Authorities and Dual-Stream Review Process

Administration of Canada's R&D tax incentives is divided between legislative policy design by the Department of Finance Canada and operational administration by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (alongside Revenu Québec for the Québec CRIC and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance for the Alberta IEG)2. Within the CRA, SR&ED claims are processed through specialized SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs)38. As documented in Tax Court jurisprudence (Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. v. The Queen, 2004 TCC) and CRA guides, submitted claims undergo initial automated and technical risk vetting; if selected for audit review, the file flows down two coordinated audit streams6:

items: Scientific/Technical Review: Conducted by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (and supervised by a Research and Technology Manager), who evaluates whether the claimed projects meet the legal requirements of subsection 248(1) and the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, and whether support work is commensurate with the needs of the experimentation7.

Financial Review: Conducted by a CRA Financial Reviewer, who reconciles Form T661 to the trial balance, payroll records, specified employee caps, client and subcontractor agreements, 180-day payment proof, assistance reductions, and Schedule T2SCH317.

body.text: 6.2 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the new optional Pre-Claim Approval Process3. This process enables eligible businesses to find out whether their planned R&D projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before they begin work or incur any costs3. Through an application (Form T1322) submitted in the CRA's My Business Account portal, a business can receive a formal pre-claim approval determination from the CRA within 8 weeks, providing upfront project certainty and a pre-claim approval case number to enter on the updated 2026 Form T6613. The CRA also provides monthly Microsoft Teams webinars, updated guidance in "The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants" explaining how claims selected for review after pre-claim approval are handled, and one-on-one pre-claim consultations via OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca3.
6.3 Complete Architecture of Form T661 (2026 Revision)

To access both the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 ITC, claimants must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals)38. According to the CRA's Guide T4088 to Form T661 and 2026 program updates, Form T661 is organized into ten parts3:

cells: Part 1
General Information (Lines 010 to 125)

Registered business or partnership name (Line 010), tax year start/end dates, 15-character Business Number (BN), total number of projects claimed (Line 050), and financial/technical contact details (Lines 100–125)38.
Part 2
Project Information (Sections A, B & C; Boxes 240, 242, 244, 246; Lines 270–282)

Project-by-project technical descriptions prepared by technical personnel38. Section A: Project identification, CRDC research code, and Pre-Claim Approval Case Number (added in 2026)6. Section B: Mandatory technical narratives for technological advancement (Box 240/246), technological uncertainty (Box 242), and systematic investigation / work performed (Box 244) (leaving these blank invalidates the project claim per Westsource, 2018 FCA 57)7. Section C: Additional project and evidence information38. (For national security "Classified Projects," Section B is kept on a separate unfiled sheet with a notice letter sent to the CRA)38.
Part 3
Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Sections A, B & C; Lines 160, 300–470)

Section A (Line 160): Irrevocable election of Proxy or Traditional Method38. Section B (Lines 300–400): Allowable SR&ED expenditures—salaries/wages (Lines 300, 305), foreign wages up to 10% (Lines 306–309), prior-year unpaid wages paid in year (Line 310), current wages unpaid at 180 days (Line 315), materials consumed (Line 320), materials transformed (Line 325), arm's-length contracts (Line 340), NAL contracts (Line 345), Traditional overhead (Line 360), third-party payments (Line 370), total current expenditures (Line 380), restored ASA capital expenditures (Line 390), and total allowable expenditures (Line 400)3. Section C (Lines 420–470): Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures38.
Part 4
Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 500 to 570)

Adds PPA (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Line 504), prior-year unpaid non-salary expenses paid in year, and NAL transferred qualified expenditures (Line 508); subtracts provincial assistance (Line 513), other government assistance (Line 515), non-government assistance/contract payments (Line 517), unpaid non-salary expenses at 180 days (Line 520), non-taxable supplier contract payments (Line 528), 20% reduction on Line 340/370 contracts and third-party payments (Line 529), prescribed excluded expenditures (Line 530), ineligible pre-Dec 16, 2024 or used capital adjustments (Line 535), and transfers to NAL payers (Line 540); adds assistance repayments (Line 560) to yield Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 570)3.
Part 5
Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (Sections A & B; Lines 810 to 820+)

Section A: Computes eligible salary base for non-specified employees (Line 810 less Line 812 bonuses/benefits) and specified employees (Line 816, applying the 75% and 2.5× YMPE caps under Reg. 2900(7)–(9))26. Section B: Computes 55% PPA (Reg. 2900(4)) and applies the Overall Cap (Reg. 2900(6))26.
Part 6
Project Costs (Part 6A Breakdown, Part 6B Capital Property, Part 6C Shared-Use Equipment)

Allocates project costs across projects; Part 6B reports the 20 most expensive post-Dec 15, 2024 ASA capital expenditures (Box 780 name, Box 782 cost, Box 786 project numbers); Part 6C reports the 20 most expensive SUE assets (Box 788 name, Box 790 YYYY-MM-DD purchase date, Box 792 25% capital cost)3.
Part 7 & Part 8
Additional Information & Claim Checklist
Statistical R&D expenditure data and completeness verification checklist38.
Part 9
Claim Preparer Information (Lines 935 to 975)

Mandatory disclosure of all external claim preparers, Business Numbers, billing arrangements, contingency fee rates, and total fees under ITA subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) (if no external preparer assisted, Lines 935, 970, and 975 must still be completed)38.
Part 10
Certification (Lines 165 to 175)
Mandatory signature by an authorized signing officer confirming compliance3.

body.text: 6.4 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline (37(11), 37(12), and 127(9)(m))

Under subsections 37(11) and 37(12) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, no amount may be deducted under Section 37 or included in an Investment Tax Credit under Section 127 unless the taxpayer files the prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information with the Minister on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year7.

Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after the end of its taxation year (while the balance of tax is due 2 months after year-end, or 3 months for qualifying CCPCs under paragraph 157(1)(b)), a corporation has an absolute statutory deadline of 18 months after the end of its taxation year to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH3113. (Electronic filing of the T2 return is mandatory under subsection 150.1(2.1), with a $1,000 penalty for paper filing under subsection 162(7.2))55. Unincorporated individuals have 17.5 months after the end of the taxation year to file Form T661 and Form T2038(IND)38.

There is no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion to extend a missed 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline13. As Canadian tax practitioners emphasize, the Taxpayer Relief provisions in subsection 220(3.1) of the ITA empower the Minister only to waive penalties and interest (such as late-filing penalties under subsection 162(1) or arrears interest under subsection 161(1)), not to revive a statute-barred SR&ED claim window under subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m)13. Furthermore, under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the ITA, claimants must retain all books, financial records, and supporting technical documentation for six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate13.

Similarly, if a claimant receives a Notice of Reassessment disallowing an SR&ED claim and wishes to object, paragraph 165(1)(b) requires a corporate taxpayer to serve a Notice of Objection within 90 days after the day of sending of the Notice of Assessment7. Under subsections 166.1(1) and (7) and subsections 166.2(1) and (5), an application to the Minister or the Tax Court of Canada for an extension of time to object cannot be granted unless the application is made within 1 year after the expiration of the 90-day objection deadline (a strict maximum of 1 year and 90 days from the mailing date of the assessment, as enforced in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146)7.
6.5 Statutory Penalties: Part 9 Preparer Penalties, Gross Negligence, and Criminal Fraud
The ITA enforces strict statutory penalties across civil and criminal tiers for non-compliant SR&ED filings:

items: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty (Subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3)): Under subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the ITA and the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, a $1,000 penalty is imposed if required information in respect of each claim preparer and billing arrangement is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate in Part 9 of Form T661 (subject to the due diligence defence in subsection 162(5.2))38. If no claim preparer assisted, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 938.

Gross Negligence and Third-Party Misrepresentation Penalties (Section 163): As warned by the CRA and tax practitioners, taxpayers are legally responsible for ensuring their claim is compliant even if misled by third-party promoters; filing unsupportable claims or misrepresenting ordinary troubleshooting as SR&ED exposes claimants to Gross Negligence Penalties under Section 163 of the ITA, as well as third-party civil penalties for misrepresentation of a tax matter by a third party3.

Criminal Prosecution for Fraudulent SR&ED Claims (Subsections 239(1.1)(a), (c), and (g)): Making false or deceptive statements in an SR&ED ITC application (239(1.1)(a)) or making false or deceptive entries in records or books of account (239(1.1)(c)) is a criminal offence7. Under paragraph 239(1.1)(g), a court must impose a criminal fine between 50% and 200% of the amount by which the claimed/requested refund or credit exceeds the amount to which the person is entitled7.

Canadian SR&ED administration and litigation are governed by an extensive body of jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), and provincial criminal courts7.
7.1 Summary Matrix of Controlling Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 252032
TCC (May 1, 1998)7
Meaning of "systematic investigation," "technological uncertainty," and "advancement"19
Taxpayer Victory (in part): Articulated the seminal 5-question test; defined routine engineering; established the 5-stage hypothesis process; held that failure reinforces technological uncertainty19.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 99 DTC 5087, Docket A-710-967
Evidentiary burden and third-party "repeatability" of test records7

Taxpayer Victory: Reversed TCC; held that requiring written records enabling third-party repeatability is an error of law where tangible technological advancement (a patented concrete panel) proves systematic testing occurred7.
116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, Docket 96-2484(IT)I7
TCC (June 9, 1998)7
Oral testimony vs. written reports under the ITA59
Taxpayer Victory: Held that while written records are strongly expected, the Act and Regulations do not prohibit adducing credible oral testimony to prove systematic SR&ED work59.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, Docket A-601-007
Software SR&ED eligibility, missing witnesses, and expert testimony7

Crown Victory: Affirmed Northwest Hydraulic; denied software claim where taxpayer kept no records, failed to call the project manager (adverse inference), and used an expert who guessed problems from the final code7.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 3557
TCC / FCA (Dec 15, 2011)7
Routine engineering in plastic thermoforming and injection moulding7

Crown Victory: Using known manufacturing processes (thermoforming/injection moulding) and heat sinks to build a lighter storage bin while managing mould costs is routine engineering, not technological advancement7.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2019 TCC 246, aff'd 2021 FCA 887
Whether "scientific method" is legally required under ITA s. 248(1)7

Crown Victory: Confirmed via purposive statutory analysis (Canada Trustco) that the Northwest Hydraulic scientific method criterion is binding law under s. 248(1) even though the exact words do not appear in the statute7.

Crown Victory: Self-imposed cost/skill limits (using SQL Server 2000 in 2011) do not create technological uncertainty; rejected after-the-fact reconstructed test tables (Exhibit A-7) and non-impartial expert advocacy7.

Weight of credible oral witness testimony vs. Minister's assumptions63

Crown Victory: Even where the Crown calls no witnesses, a credible taxpayer witness does not displace the Minister's SR&ED assumptions unless the testimony establishes the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria56.

System uncertainty in heavy CNC machine tool design & failed projects7

Taxpayer Victory (Divided): Allowed $435,842 ITCs in 2007 for 80-ton custom lathe and 100% of ITCs in 2006–2008 for an abandoned double-wheel roll grinder where severe vibration and scale created system uncertainty7.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 777
SR&ED eligibility after premature commercial release and product recall7

Taxpayer Victory: Commercial release of 200 miniature wireless printers did not bar subsequent SR&ED claims when a >20% failure rate revealed unresolved system-level battery and paper-curling uncertainties7.

Taxpayer Victory: Upheld shop-floor SR&ED claims for electric motor/appliance subassembly manufacturing, highlighting the decisive value of independent expert witness testimony60.

Taxpayer Victory (Capped): Qualified $387,553 of SR&ED expenditures for high-pressure HVAC integration, but relief was statutorily capped at $12,000 for 2008 because the taxpayer elected the Informal Procedure7.

Crown Victory: Shop-floor trial-and-error using standard hydraulic valves and hand cranks without P.Eng. analysis or kept records of failed designs is routine engineering, not SR&ED7.
Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 217
Paper formulations and literature reviews without clinical/lab trials7

Crown Victory: Literature searches, theoretical paper formulations of natural health products, and Health Canada regulatory communications without systematic experimental testing do not qualify as applied research7.
Murray Arlin Dentistry PC v. The Queen, 2012 TCC 1337
Automated database tracking vs. pre-formulated hypotheses7

Crown Victory: Generating automated comparative implant tables from commercial dental software without pre-formulated hypotheses or contemporaneous time records is not SR&ED; no leniency for first-time claimants7.
Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211, aff'd 2016 FCA 3017
Late filing of Schedule T2SCH31 after timely filing of Form T6617

Crown Victory: Filing Form T661 on time (June 30) but filing Schedule 31 six weeks late (August 16) is fatal under ITA para. 127(9)(m); s. 32 of the Interpretation Act cannot rescue an unfiled schedule7.
Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 9, aff'd 2018 FCA 577
Filing Form T661 on time with Boxes 240, 242, and 244 left blank7

Crown Victory: Leaving project technical narrative Boxes 240, 242, and 244 blank on Form T661 violates ss. 37(11) and 37(12) and invalidates the claim, even if a related company's claim for the same project was approved7.
1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 5117
Proof of timely delivery of T661 technical project report7

Crown Victory: Dismissed claim where T661 financial pages had a timely March 28 CRA "received" stamp but the file copy of the technical report lacked a stamp and was faxed after the March 31 deadline7.
CAE Inc. v. The King, 2021 TCC 57, aff'd 2022 FCA 1787
Whether repayable federal SADI loans constitute "government assistance"7

Crown Victory: Unconditionally repayable federal SADI loans with below-market implicit return rates are not ordinary commercial loans and constitute "government assistance" under s. 127(9), reducing SR&ED ITCs on full principal7.
CCLC Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 96 DTC 6527, Docket A-801-957
Government research funding with conditional equity buy-back7

Crown Victory: Provincial funding under a Coal Research Agreement where the government earned no commercial net profit upon success was "government assistance" under s. 127(9) and 12(1)(x), not an ordinary business investment7.
Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen, 94 DTC 1725, Docket 92-2647
Timeframe for evaluating the "All or Substantially All" (ASA) capital test7

Taxpayer Victory: The ASA (90%+) test for SR&ED capital equipment must be evaluated based on intention and use during the prosecution of SR&ED, not penalized years later because a successful prototype enters commercial use7.
Fio Corporation v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 587
CRA use of pre-trial discovery documents to issue new reassessments7

Taxpayer Victory: The common-law implied undertaking rule bars the CRA from using documents obtained in Tax Court discovery to reassess other years without leave of the Court; awarded $25,000 costs against the Crown7.
R. v. Elhami & Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc., 2017 QCCQ 26847
Court of Québec (Mar 27, 2017)7
Criminal prosecution under ITA s. 239(1.1) for fabricated SR&ED invoices7

Crown Conviction: Imposed $3,972,882 in total criminal fines ($1,324,294 on each of 3 co-defendants, equal to 100% of the falsely requested ITC) for submitting fake $4.5M subcontractor invoices, even though the CRA paid out nothing7.

body.text: 7.2 Detailed Doctrinal Analysis of Key Judicial Precedents
1. The Foundational Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998 TCC)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), Judge Donald Bowman (as he then was) articulated the five criteria at paragraph 16 that govern every SR&ED eligibility dispute in Canada32. Under the first criterion (technological risk or uncertainty), the court asks whether there was an uncertainty that could not be removed by "routine engineering or standard procedures," which Judge Bowman defined as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field32. Under the second criterion (formulation of hypotheses), the claimant must demonstrate a five-stage process: (a) observation of the subject matter of the problem, (b) formulation of a clear objective, (c) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, (d) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses19. Under the third criterion (scientific method), the procedures adopted must accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses7. Under the fourth criterion (technological advancement), the process must seek an advancement in "general understanding"—meaning something known to, or available to, persons knowledgeable in the field (rather than a piece of knowledge known secretly to someone somewhere)32. Crucially, Judge Bowman held that if the initial objective is not achieved, that failure invalidates neither the hypothesis formed nor the methods used; on the contrary, "it is possible that the very failure reinforces the measure of the technological uncertainty"19. Under the fifth criterion (contemporaneous records), the taxpayer is expected to keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progresses34.
2. Appellate Confirmation of the Scientific Method and Contemporaneous Evidence: RIS-Christie, 116736 Canada Inc., C.W. Agencies, Kam-Press, National R&D, and Tuna Temple

While Justice Archambault noted in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (1998 TCC) that the ITA and Regulations do not contain an absolute statutory prohibition against proving SR&ED through credible oral testimony where written reports are incomplete59, and the Federal Court of Appeal held in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada (1998 FCA) that a trial judge errs in law by demanding written test logs that satisfy a third-party "repeatability" standard when a patented concrete forming panel proves technological advancement was achieved7, subsequent appellate decisions demonstrate that lacking contemporaneous records of systematic experimentation is almost always fatal in contested software and industrial claims7.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393), the appellant claimed SR&ED credits for 1991–1995 for developing an in-house International Distributed Lottery System (IDLS) handling 25,000 orders per day7. The FCA dismissed the appeal, affirming Judge Bonner's findings that the appellant retained no documentation to rebut the Minister's assumptions, failed to call the project manager or key developers to testify (warranting an adverse inference that their testimony would not have been helpful), and relied on an expert witness who was handicapped into guessing what problems occurred by examining the finished software, whereas the Crown's expert (Dr. Takagaki) demonstrated that the system was built using standard software engineering7.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88, aff'g 2019 TCC 246, where the appellant used 3D CAD modelling and factory mock-ups to build curved tempered-glass memorial niche columns) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, aff'g 2020 TCC 47), the appellants argued that because the phrase "scientific method" does not appear in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic should not apply7. The Federal Court of Appeal unanimously rejected this contention in both appeals (citing its prior endorsements in RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel Manufacturing, and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 152), holding that under purposive statutory interpretation (Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54), the Northwest Hydraulic five-part test is the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1)7. In National R&D, the taxpayer (an SR&ED consulting firm) claimed $68,029 in expenditures for developing a web-based Project Tracking System using Classic ASP, COM+, and Microsoft SQL Server 2000 in 2011—imposing a self-restricted budget and skill constraint to use only legacy tools the owner already owned7. Justice Lafleur (affirmed by Justice Rennie at the FCA) held that the issues were solvable by routine engineering, refused to qualify the appellant's hired expert (noting an expert's overriding duty of impartiality to the court), and rejected Exhibit A-7 (a list of 50 grouped experiments) after the owner admitted on cross-examination that it was created after the fact for the CRA review7. Similarly, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175), the FCA confirmed that even when the Crown calls no witnesses and the taxpayer's witness is found credible, credible oral testimony alone does not displace the Minister's assumptions unless it substantively proves the Northwest Hydraulic criteria56.
3. System Uncertainty, Shop-Floor R&D, and Post-Release Failures: A&D Precision, 6379249 Canada Inc., Airmax, Les Abeilles, Jentel, Joel Theatrical, Life Choice, and Murray Arlin
Canadian courts carefully distinguish genuine system uncertainty from routine trial-and-error manufacturing:

items: Qualifying System-Level and Shop-Floor SR&ED: In A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen (2019 TCC 48), a Concord, Ontario high-precision machining company built custom "Matteo" CNC horizontal lathes to machine 80-ton to 100-ton gas turbine rotors for General Electric and attempted to build a double-wheel roll grinding machine7. Supported by expert testimony from Dr. Stephen Veldhuis and Dr. Eu-Gene Ng, Justice Russell allowed $435,842 of ITCs in 2007 for the 80-ton lathe, one-third of the 2008 lathe ITCs, and 100% of the 2006–2008 ITCs for the double-wheel roll grinder, even though A&D ultimately abandoned the grinder due to persistent spindle vibration and overheating7. In 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77), CEO and inventor Raja Tuli released 200 units of a miniature wireless portable printer (1.5 in × 1.5 in × 10 in) at the end of 2008, only to recall the product when >20% failed due to paper curling and battery drain after 5 to 10 pages7. Justice D'Auray rejected the CRA's position that commercial release terminated SR&ED eligibility, holding that unresolved system-level uncertainties persisted in 2009 and 2010 and allowing the appeal with costs7. In 1726437 Ontario Inc. o/a Airmax Technologies v. The Queen (2012 TCC 376), Justice Hogan qualified $387,553 of SR&ED expenditures for resolving high-static-pressure HVAC system integration uncertainties (adapting a European boiler, reprogramming a Korean ECM fan motor, and perforating flexible ducts to drop noise from 60 dB to 40 dB), though the 2008 refundable ITC judgment was capped at $12,000 under Section 18.1 of the Tax Court of Canada Act (Innovations et Intégrations Brassicoles Inc. v. The Queen, 2009 FCA 302) because the appellant used the Informal Procedure7.

Disallowed Routine Engineering and Post-Hoc Claims: Conversely, in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355), using well-known plastic thermoforming and injection moulding processes with a heat sink to build a lighter storage bin was held to be routine engineering7. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), testing combinations of hydraulic pumps, hoses, and valves for theatre fire curtains and adding a hand-crank override without any professional engineer involvement—and deliberately discarding failed design sketches so employees would not build them, while relying on summary sheets written after the fact by a tax consultant—was dismissed as routine trial-and-error troubleshooting7. Likewise, in Life Choice Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 21), conducting medical literature reviews and paper formulations for natural health products (amygdalin/B12, neuro support, and oral EDTA alternatives) while skipping clinical or animal trials was held not to constitute systematic experimentation or analysis7. And in Murray Arlin Dentistry PC v. The Queen (2012 TCC 133), a periodontist who claimed 1/5th of his salary ($70,000 plus $45,000 proxy) for tracking 12,000 dental implants in commercial Tritan software lost his appeal because generating comparative tables at the push of a button without pre-formulated hypotheses or reliable time records did not constitute SR&ED, and Justice Woods confirmed that first-time claimants receive no special leniency on evidentiary proof7.

body.text: 4. Strict Procedural Compliance, Government Assistance, Discovery Protection, and Criminal Fraud: Easy Way Cattle Oilers, Westsource, One Source Metal, CAE Inc., CCLC, Highland Foundry, Fio Corp., and Tempora

items: Fatal Filing Defects (Easy Way Cattle Oilers, Westsource, and One Source Metal): In Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen (2016 FCA 301, aff'g 2015 TCC 211), the taxpayer filed its 2008 T2 return and Form T661 on time (by June 30, 2010), and the CRA accepted $95,791 of allowable SR&ED expenditures, but the taxpayer's accountants filed Schedule T2SCH31 late on August 16, 20107. The FCA held that Schedule T2SCH31 is the sole prescribed form authorized under paragraph 127(9)(m) and subsection 244(16) to claim an ITC, and Section 32 of the Interpretation Act cannot convert Form T661 into an ITC claim form7. In Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen (2018 FCA 57, aff'g 2017 TCC 9), the FCA held that leaving Boxes 240, 242, and 244 blank on Form T661 is fatal under subsections 37(11) and 37(12), even when a related corporation's T661 for the exact same project was accepted by the CRA7. And in 1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. The Queen (2009 TCC 511), Justice Bowie dismissed a 2005 appeal where the accountant's courier obtained a timely March 28, 2007 CRA date-stamp on the file copies of the 2005 and 2006 T661 forms, but the file copy of the supporting Technical Report had no date-stamp and CRA logs showed it was only faxed on April 12, 2007 (after the March 31, 2007 deadline)7.

Broad Scope of "Government Assistance" (CAE Inc. and CCLC Technologies): In CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178, aff'g 2021 TCC 57), the FCA held that unconditionally repayable federal contributions under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) program for "Project Falcon" constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) because the loan's implicit rate of return was below commercial market rates, and confirmed that the entire loan principal (not merely the interest rate differential) reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures and is included in income (applying The Queen v. Consumers' Gas Co., CCLC Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 96 DTC 6527 (FCA), and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196)7.

Capital Equipment ASA Timing (Highland Foundry) and Discovery Protection (Fio Corporation): In Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen (94 DTC 1725, TCC), the Tax Court held that the "all or substantially all" (90%+) test for SR&ED capital expenditures (a prototype green-sand reclamation refiner and lab testing equipment) must be evaluated at the time the expenditure is incurred and during the period in which SR&ED is prosecuted, not denied retroactively using hindsight because the successful prototype continued to be used in commercial foundry operations for years7. In Fio Corporation v. The Queen (2014 TCC 58), Justice D'Arcy ruled that the common-law implied undertaking rule (Juman v. Doucette) applies to the CRA in Tax Court appeals and is not overridden by Section 241 of the ITA: when Fio Corp. voluntarily disclosed 260 documents in seven binders during pre-trial discovery for its 2007–2008 SR&ED appeal and the CRA used those discovery documents to issue new reassessments, the Court prohibited the Crown from using any discovery-obtained documents in other proceedings without leave of the Court and awarded $25,000 in costs to the taxpayer7.

Criminal Fines on Unpaid Fraudulent Claims (R. v. Elhami & Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc.): In R. v. Elhami, Elhami & Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc. (2017 QCCQ 2684), the three co-defendants submitted two fabricated, antedated invoices totalling over $4,500,000 allegedly from Pyro Genesis (which had never performed the work) to claim $1,324,294 in SR&ED ITCs, and attempted to persuade Pyro Genesis to stage equipment for a CRA site visit7. Although the CRA detected the fraud during audit and disbursed $0, the Court of Québec (Criminal and Penal Chamber) rejected the defence argument that the fine should be based on the $0 obtained, holding that paragraph 239(1.1)(g) mandates a fine of 50% to 200% of the requested credit ($1,324,294) and imposing a $1,324,294 fine on each of the three co-defendants (a combined criminal fine pool of $3,972,882)7.

body.text: 8. Audit Defence Playbook and Contemporaneous Documentation Standards

To ensure full compliance and audit readiness across both CRA scientific (RTA) and financial reviews in 2026, Canadian enterprises and their tax advisors should execute the following eight-step verification protocol6:

items: Contemporaneous Technical Evidence Capture: Establish an operating system where engineers and scientists record technological uncertainties, hypotheses, experimental plans, and test results as the work occurs rather than reconstructing narratives after year-end (National R&D, 2022 FCA 72)6. Preserve all evidence of failed trials, negative test data, and aborted prototypes rather than deleting or discarding them (Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6)6.

Proactive Use of Pre-Claim Approval (Form T1322): For new or high-expenditure R&D projects commencing on or after April 1, 2026, submit an optional Pre-Claim Approval application (Form T1322) via My Business Account prior to starting work to obtain an 8-week CRA eligibility determination and case number for Form T6613.

Methodological Selection Arithmetic (Proxy vs. Traditional): Perform an annual comparative calculation before filing the initial Form T661 (Line 160) to determine whether the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Reg. 2900(4)) exceeds actual directly related and incremental SR&ED overhead (such as dedicated experimental cloud compute clusters, which can only be claimed under the Traditional Method on Line 360)13.

Trial Balance and Payroll Reconciliation: Reconcile all Form T661 expenditure lines to the financial statement trial balance, general ledger, and T4 summaries prior to filing13. Maintain monthly per-employee percentage time-tracking logs separating hands-on "directly engaged" SR&ED time (and commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work) from commercial production and routine debugging (which also drives the Québec CRIC exclusion threshold)15.

Owner-Manager (Specified Employee) Compliance: Pay founders via T4 salary rather than dividends; strip all bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits from specified employee claims (37(9) and Reg. 2900(9)); apply the 5× YMPE direct salary cap ($373,000 in 2026 under 37(9.1)) and the lesser of 75% of total salary or 2.5× YMPE proxy base cap ($186,500 in 2026 under Reg. 2900(7)); and file allocation agreements across associated corporations (37(9.2)–(9.4) and 127(10.3))9.

Restored Capital Equipment and Lease Logs (Post-December 15, 2024): For depreciable capital property (Line 390, Part 6B), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504, Part 6C), and leased equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, maintain contemporaneous equipment-use operating logs substantiating ≥90% ASA operating time (or >50% to <90% primary use for SUE), document available-for-use dates, exclude Line 390 ASA capital from Schedule T2SCH8 CCA, and track assets for 20 years for potential ITC recapture under subsection 127(27)3.

Subcontractor Statements of Work and 180-Day Cash Settlement: Ensure all subcontractor contracts and invoices explicitly state that the R&D or pre-commercialization work was performed in Canada (or in Québec for the 50% CRIC subcontractor claim) and link directly to the SR&ED project6. Verify that all accrued wages (Line 315) and non-salary current expenditures (Line 520) are paid within 180 days of fiscal year-end (78(4) and 127(26))9.

Prescribed Form and Deadline Verification: Ensure that Form T661 (with Boxes 240/242/244/246 and Part 9 Claim Preparer Information fully completed and date-stamped/transmitted), Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)), and all provincial schedules (Schedule 566, Schedule 508, Schedules 568/569, Form RD-1029.8.CR, Form T666, Schedule 403, Schedule 380, Schedule 340, Schedule 360, Schedule 301, Schedule 442) are filed before the absolute, non-extendable 18-month reporting deadline (37(11) and 127(9)(m))4.
